title: Paul Brunton
subtitle: The philosopher who brought Ramana Maharshi to the West.
meta_description: Paul Brunton (1898–1981) was the British philosopher and author who first brought Sri Ramana Maharshi to the attention of the Western world through his 1934 book A Search in Secret India. Ramana himself said: 'Paul Brunton is one of my eyes. My shakti is working through him.'
body_html:
The Search Begins

Paul Brunton was born Raphael Hurst in London in 1898. A journalist, mystic and restless seeker, he spent the 1920s and early 1930s travelling through Egypt, Greece and the East in search of something that neither Western philosophy nor occultism had been able to provide — an experience of the Real.

In 1930 he arrived in India, armed with letters of introduction and a journalist's sceptical eye. He visited yogis, fakirs and holy men of every kind, and found most of them wanting. Then, almost as an afterthought, a friend mentioned a silent sage on a hill in South India.

The Meeting at Arunachala

Brunton's first meeting with Sri Ramana Maharshi in the early 1930s became one of the most consequential encounters in the history of modern spirituality. He described arriving in the Maharshi's hall with his notebook ready, full of prepared questions — and finding that the questions dissolved before they could be asked.

"I had gone to an Indian master expecting to find a learned pundit who would expound abstruse doctrines, and I had found a simple man who sat in silence and whose silence spoke more eloquently than any words."

Over several visits, Brunton experienced something he later described as the deepest stillness he had ever known — a silence that was not empty but full, a presence that answered every question by dissolving the questioner.

A Search in Secret India

Published in 1934, A Search in Secret India introduced Sri Ramana Maharshi — and the practice of Self-enquiry — to readers in Britain, America and across the Western world for the first time. The book became an immediate success and has never been out of print.

Ramana's response to the book was characteristically simple. When visitors mentioned it, he smiled. When pressed for his view of Brunton's account, he confirmed its accuracy. And to one visitor who asked directly about the author, he said something that became famous among those who knew him:

"Paul Brunton is one of my 'eyes.' My shakti is working through him. Follow him closely."

— Sri Ramana Maharshi

The Notebooks of Paul Brunton

After A Search in Secret India, Brunton continued writing, publishing works on the Maharshi's teachings, on Indian philosophy, and on what he called the Overself — his term for the impersonal witness-consciousness that Ramana pointed to as the Self.

In his final decades, he withdrew from public life and devoted himself entirely to a vast private notebook project — meditations, philosophical paragraphs and teaching notes accumulated over fifty years of practice. These were published posthumously as the sixteen-volume Notebooks of Paul Brunton (1984–1988).

The Notebooks return again and again to what Brunton called The Short Path: the direct, immediate recognition of what is already present, as distinct from the Long Path of gradual purification and practice. In this, his mature teaching converges precisely with Ramana Maharshi's pointing.

"The Short Path is the recognition that the Overself is not something to be attained in the future but something that is already present, always present — that which is looking through your eyes right now."

Legacy

Paul Brunton died in 1981 in Vevey, Switzerland, at the age of 83. His work is archived and continued by the Paul Brunton Philosophic Foundation, which maintains his notebooks, correspondence and unpublished writings.

Of all the Western writers who encountered Ramana Maharshi, Brunton stands alone in having received the Maharshi's explicit endorsement. His A Search in Secret India remains, nine decades later, the single most widely read introduction to the sage of Arunachala.
